--- title: "Linear Regression 📈" subtitle: "MATH 4750 / MSSC 5750 Computational Statistics" format: revealjs: code-line-numbers: false html-math-method: method: mathjax url: "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/mathjax@3/es5/tex-mml-chtml.js" highlight-style: arrow code-block-bg: true self-contained: false slide-number: c/t incremental: false width: 1800 height: 1000 margin: 0.05 logo: "logo.png" footer: "[mmadoliat.github.io/compstat-s27](https://mmadoliat.github.io/compstat-s27/)" theme: ["simple", "slides.scss"] multiplex: false code-link: true fig-cap-location: bottom fig-align: center transition: none ## fade slide convex concave zoom title-slide-attributes: data-background-image: mu-bg.png data-background-size: stretch data-slide-number: none editor: source execute: freeze: auto echo: true purl: true --- # {visibility="hidden"} \def\bx{\mathbf{x}} \def\by{\mathbf{y}} \def\bz{\mathbf{z}} \def\bu{\mathbf{u}} \def\bv{\mathbf{v}} \def\bw{\mathbf{w}} \def\bX{\mathbf{X}} \def\bY{\mathbf{Y}} \def\bZ{\mathbf{Z}} \def\bU{\mathbf{U}} \def\bV{\mathbf{V}} \def\bW{\mathbf{W}} \def\bI{\mathbf{I}} \def\bH{\mathbf{H}} \def\bS{\mathbf{S}} \def\bD{\mathbf{D}} \def\bbeta{\boldsymbol \beta} \def\btheta{\boldsymbol \theta} \def\bmu{\boldsymbol \mu} \def\bSigma{\boldsymbol \Sigma} \def\bLambda{\boldsymbol \Lambda} \def\beps{\boldsymbol \epsilon} \def\T{\text{T}} \def\E{\mathrm{E}} \def\var{\mathrm{Var}} \def\cov{\mathrm{Cov}} \def\cor{\mathrm{Corr}} \def\se{\mathrm{se}} \def\bias{\mathrm{bias}} \def\mse{\mathrm{MSE}} \def\R{\mathbb{R}} \def\P{\mathrm{P}} \def\iid{\stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim}} \DeclareMathOperator*{\argmin}{arg\,min} \DeclareMathOperator*{\argmax}{arg\,max} # Linear Regression

The linear regression model and least squares

Accuracy of coefficients and of the model

Qualitative predictors and interactions

Potential problems

Linear regression vs. KNN regression

::: notes - Based on Chapter 3 of *An Introduction to Statistical Learning* (James, Witten, Hastie, Tibshirani), . - In this course we look at regression with a computational eye: matrix computations, simulation of sampling distributions, and nonparametric competitors. ::: ## Linear Regression - A simple approach to **supervised learning**: assume the dependence of $Y$ on $X_1,\dots,X_p$ is linear. - True regression functions are never exactly linear! ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750) f <- function(x) 4 + 0.35 * x + 0.6 * sin(x) x <- seq(1.5, 8.5, length = 100) plot(x, f(x), type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "red", ylab = "f(x)") abline(lm(f(x) ~ x), lwd = 3, col = "blue") legend("topleft", c("true f(x)", "best linear approximation"), col = c("red", "blue"), lwd = 3, bty = "n") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/03-regression/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: - Although it may seem overly simplistic, linear regression is extremely useful both conceptually and practically. ## Advertising Data ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} Advertising <- read.csv("data/Advertising.csv")[, -1] par(mfrow = c(1, 3)) for (v in c("TV", "radio", "newspaper")) { plot(Advertising[[v]], Advertising$sales, pch = 20, col = "#C0392B80", xlab = v, ylab = "sales") abline(lm(Advertising$sales ~ Advertising[[v]]), col = "blue", lwd = 3) } ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/03-regression/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: question Is there a relationship between budget and sales? How strong? Which media contribute? How accurately can we predict future sales? Is it linear? Is there synergy? ::: ## Simple Linear Regression $$ Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X + \epsilon $$ - $\beta_0, \beta_1$: unknown **intercept** and **slope** (coefficients, parameters); $\epsilon$: error term. - Given estimates, predict with $\hat y = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 x$. **Least squares.** With residuals $e_i = y_i - \hat y_i$, minimize $\text{RSS} = e_1^2 + \dots + e_n^2$: $$ \hat\beta_1 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)}{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\bar x)^2},\qquad \hat\beta_0 = \bar y - \hat\beta_1\bar x. $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- Advertising$TV; y <- Advertising$sales b1 <- sum((x - mean(x)) * (y - mean(y))) / sum((x - mean(x))^2) b0 <- mean(y) - b1 * mean(x) c(b0 = b0, b1 = b1); coef(lm(sales ~ TV, data = Advertising)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` b0 b1 7.03259 0.04754 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (Intercept) TV 7.03259 0.04754 ``` ::: ::: ## Least Squares Fit for `sales` onto `TV` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} fit_tv <- lm(sales ~ TV, data = Advertising) plot(sales ~ TV, data = Advertising, pch = 20, col = "red") segments(Advertising$TV, Advertising$sales, Advertising$TV, fitted(fit_tv), col = "gray50") abline(fit_tv, col = "blue", lwd = 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/03-regression/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: A linear fit captures the essence of the relationship, although it is somewhat deficient in the left of the plot. ## The RSS Surface ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} rss <- function(b0, b1) sum((y - b0 - b1 * x)^2) b0g <- seq(5, 9, length = 60); b1g <- seq(0.03, 0.065, length = 60) z <- outer(b0g, b1g, Vectorize(rss)) par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) contour(b0g, b1g, z / 1000, nlevels = 15, xlab = expression(beta[0]), ylab = expression(beta[1])) points(b0, b1, pch = 19, col = "red", cex = 2) persp(b0g, b1g, z / 1000, theta = 30, phi = 25, col = "#FFCC00", border = NA, shade = 0.5, xlab = "b0", ylab = "b1", zlab = "RSS/1000") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/03-regression/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Accuracy of the Coefficient Estimates $$ \se(\hat\beta_1)^2 = \frac{\sigma^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2},\qquad \se(\hat\beta_0)^2 = \sigma^2\left[\frac1n + \frac{\bar x^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\bar x)^2}\right],\qquad \sigma^2 = \var(\epsilon). $$ - An approximate 95% **confidence interval**: $\hat\beta_1 \pm 2\cdot\se(\hat\beta_1)$. ::: question What does "95% confidence" mean? Let's *simulate* repeated samples from a known model. ::: ## Simulating the Sampling Distribution of $\hat\beta_1$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750) beta0 <- 2; beta1 <- 3; sigma <- 2; xs <- runif(100, -2, 2) # fixed design sims <- t(replicate(2000, { ys <- beta0 + beta1 * xs + rnorm(100, sd = sigma) ft <- summary(lm(ys ~ xs))$coefficients c(est = ft[2, 1], se = ft[2, 2]) })) c(sd_of_estimates = sd(sims[, "est"]), theory = sigma / sqrt(sum((xs - mean(xs))^2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` sd_of_estimates theory 0.1709 0.1691 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} covered <- abs(sims[, "est"] - beta1) <= qt(.975, 98) * sims[, "se"] mean(covered) # empirical coverage ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.95 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} hist(sims[, "est"], breaks = 40, col = "#FFCC00", main = expression(paste("2000 draws of ", hat(beta)[1]))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/03-regression/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Hypothesis Testing and the $t$ Statistic $$ H_0: \beta_1 = 0 \quad\text{(no relationship)}\qquad\text{vs}\qquad H_A: \beta_1\neq 0 $$ $$ t = \frac{\hat\beta_1 - 0}{\se(\hat\beta_1)} \sim t_{n-2}\ \text{under } H_0 $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(fit_tv)$coefficients ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 7.03259 0.457843 15.36 1.406e-35 TV 0.04754 0.002691 17.67 1.467e-42 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} confint(fit_tv) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 2.5 % 97.5 % (Intercept) 6.12972 7.93547 TV 0.04223 0.05284 ``` ::: ::: ## Assessing the Overall Accuracy of the Model - **Residual standard error:** $\text{RSE} = \sqrt{\text{RSS}/(n-2)}$ - **$R^2$** $= \dfrac{\text{TSS}-\text{RSS}}{\text{TSS}} = 1 - \dfrac{\text{RSS}}{\text{TSS}}$, $\quad \text{TSS} = \sum(y_i-\bar y)^2$ - In simple regression, $R^2 = r^2 = \cor(X,Y)^2$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} RSS <- sum(resid(fit_tv)^2); TSS <- sum((y - mean(y))^2) c(RSE = sqrt(RSS / (length(y) - 2)), R2 = 1 - RSS / TSS, r2 = cor(x, y)^2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` RSE R2 r2 3.2587 0.6119 0.6119 ``` ::: ::: # Multiple Linear Regression ## The Model and Its Matrix Form $$ Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1X_1 + \cdots + \beta_pX_p + \epsilon, \qquad \by = \bX\bbeta + \beps $$ $$ \hat\bbeta = \argmin_{\bbeta}\|\by - \bX\bbeta\|^2 = (\bX^\T\bX)^{-1}\bX^\T\by $$ - Interpret $\beta_j$ as the average effect on $Y$ of a one-unit increase in $X_j$, **holding all other predictors fixed**. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} X <- cbind(1, as.matrix(Advertising[, c("TV", "radio", "newspaper")])) bhat_normal <- solve(t(X) %*% X, t(X) %*% Advertising$sales) # normal equations bhat_qr <- qr.coef(qr(X), Advertising$sales) # what lm() actually does cbind(bhat_normal, bhat_qr) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` bhat_qr 2.938889 2.938889 TV 0.045765 0.045765 radio 0.188530 0.188530 newspaper -0.001037 -0.001037 ``` ::: ::: ::: notes - lm uses a QR decomposition, which is numerically more stable than solving the normal equations (Chapter 13). ::: ## Results for the Advertising Data ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} fit3 <- lm(sales ~ TV + radio + newspaper, data = Advertising) summary(fit3)$coefficients ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 2.938889 0.311908 9.4223 1.267e-17 TV 0.045765 0.001395 32.8086 1.510e-81 radio 0.188530 0.008611 21.8935 1.505e-54 newspaper -0.001037 0.005871 -0.1767 8.599e-01 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} round(cor(Advertising), 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` TV radio newspaper sales TV 1.000 0.055 0.057 0.782 radio 0.055 1.000 0.354 0.576 newspaper 0.057 0.354 1.000 0.228 sales 0.782 0.576 0.228 1.000 ``` ::: ::: ::: question `newspaper` is significant on its own but not in the multiple regression. Why? Look at the correlation between `radio` and `newspaper`. ::: ## Is At Least One Predictor Useful? The $F$ Test $$ H_0:\beta_1 = \cdots = \beta_p = 0,\qquad F = \frac{(\text{TSS}-\text{RSS})/p}{\text{RSS}/(n-p-1)}\sim F_{p,\,n-p-1} $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} anova(lm(sales ~ 1, data = Advertising), fit3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Analysis of Variance Table Model 1: sales ~ 1 Model 2: sales ~ TV + radio + newspaper Res.Df RSS Df Sum of Sq F Pr(>F) 1 199 5417 2 196 557 3 4860 570 <2e-16 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ::: - **Deciding on important variables:** all subsets ($2^p$ models!), forward, backward selection; use $C_p$, AIC, BIC, adjusted $R^2$, or cross-validation (Ch 8). ## Prediction: Confidence vs. Prediction Intervals ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} fit2 <- lm(sales ~ TV + radio, data = Advertising) new <- data.frame(TV = 100, radio = 20) predict(fit2, new, interval = "confidence") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` fit lwr upr 1 11.26 10.99 11.53 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} predict(fit2, new, interval = "prediction") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` fit lwr upr 1 11.26 7.93 14.58 ``` ::: ::: - **Confidence interval:** uncertainty about $f(X) = \E[Y\mid X]$ (reducible error). - **Prediction interval:** also includes the irreducible error $\epsilon$, so it is always wider. # Other Considerations ## Qualitative Predictors ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ISLR2) str(Credit[, c("Balance", "Income", "Student", "Region", "Own")]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 'data.frame': 400 obs. of 5 variables: $ Balance: num 333 903 580 964 331 ... $ Income : num 14.9 106 104.6 148.9 55.9 ... $ Student: Factor w/ 2 levels "No","Yes": 1 2 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 2 ... $ Region : Factor w/ 3 levels "East","South",..: 2 3 3 3 2 2 1 3 2 1 ... $ Own : Factor w/ 2 levels "No","Yes": 1 2 1 2 1 1 2 1 2 2 ... ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} summary(lm(Balance ~ Own, data = Credit))$coefficients ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 509.80 33.13 15.3889 2.909e-42 OwnYes 19.73 46.05 0.4285 6.685e-01 ``` ::: ::: - A factor with $k$ levels enters through $k-1$ **dummy variables**; the baseline is absorbed into the intercept. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} head(model.matrix(~ Region, data = Credit), 4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (Intercept) RegionSouth RegionWest 1 1 1 0 2 1 0 1 3 1 0 1 4 1 0 1 ``` ::: ::: ## Interactions: Advertising Data $$ \texttt{sales} = \beta_0+\beta_1\texttt{TV}+\beta_2\texttt{radio}+\beta_3(\texttt{radio}\times\texttt{TV}) + \epsilon = \beta_0 + (\beta_1+\beta_3\,\texttt{radio})\texttt{TV} + \beta_2\texttt{radio} + \epsilon $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} fit_int <- lm(sales ~ TV * radio, data = Advertising) summary(fit_int)$coefficients ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 6.750220 2.479e-01 27.233 1.541e-68 TV 0.019101 1.504e-03 12.699 2.364e-27 radio 0.028860 8.905e-03 3.241 1.400e-03 TV:radio 0.001086 5.242e-05 20.727 2.758e-51 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} c(R2_additive = summary(fit2)$r.squared, R2_interaction = summary(fit_int)$r.squared) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` R2_additive R2_interaction 0.8972 0.9678 ``` ::: ::: - The interaction explains $(96.8-89.7)/(100-89.7)\approx 69\%$ of the variability left after the additive model. - A $\$1{,}000$ increase in TV is associated with $(\hat\beta_1 + \hat\beta_3\times\texttt{radio})\times 1000$ more units sold. ## The Hierarchy Principle ::: alert If we include an interaction in a model, we should also include the main effects, even if the $p$-values associated with their coefficients are not significant. ::: - Interactions are hard to interpret in a model without main effects; their meaning changes. - The interaction terms also contain main effects if the model has no main-effect terms. ## Qualitative $\times$ Quantitative Interactions: Credit Data ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} f_add <- lm(Balance ~ Income + Student, data = Credit) f_int <- lm(Balance ~ Income * Student, data = Credit) par(mfrow = c(1, 2)); inc <- 0:150 for (f in list(f_add, f_int)) { plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 150), ylim = c(200, 1500), xlab = "Income", ylab = "Balance", main = if (identical(f, f_add)) "no interaction" else "with interaction") lines(inc, predict(f, data.frame(Income = inc, Student = "Yes")), col = "red", lwd = 3) lines(inc, predict(f, data.frame(Income = inc, Student = "No")), lwd = 3) } ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/03-regression/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Non-linear Effects: Polynomial Regression on `Auto` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(mpg ~ horsepower, data = Auto, col = "gray50", pch = 1) hp <- seq(40, 230, length = 200) cols <- c("orange", "#3D85C6", "#00A087") for (k in seq_along(c(1, 2, 5))) { d <- c(1, 2, 5)[k] lines(hp, predict(lm(mpg ~ poly(horsepower, d), data = Auto), data.frame(horsepower = hp)), lwd = 3, col = cols[k]) } legend("topright", c("Linear", "Degree 2", "Degree 5"), col = cols, lwd = 3, bty = "n") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/03-regression/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} summary(lm(mpg ~ horsepower + I(horsepower^2), data = Auto))$coefficients ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 56.900100 1.8004268 31.60 1.741e-109 horsepower -0.466190 0.0311246 -14.98 2.289e-40 I(horsepower^2) 0.001231 0.0001221 10.08 2.196e-21 ``` ::: ::: # Potential Problems ## Six Things That Can Go Wrong :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="45%"} 1. Non-linearity of the response-predictor relationship 2. Correlation of error terms 3. Non-constant variance of errors 4. Outliers 5. High-leverage points 6. Collinearity ::: ::: {.column width="55%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1)) plot(lm(mpg ~ horsepower, data = Auto), which = c(1, 3, 5, 2), pch = 20, col = "#00336680") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/03-regression/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Collinearity and the Variance Inflation Factor $$ \text{VIF}(\hat\beta_j) = \frac{1}{1-R^2_{X_j\mid X_{-j}}} $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} vif <- function(fit) { X <- model.matrix(fit)[, -1] sapply(seq_len(ncol(X)), function(j) 1 / (1 - summary(lm(X[, j] ~ X[, -j]))$r.squared)) |> setNames(colnames(X)) } round(vif(lm(Balance ~ Age + Limit + Rating, data = Credit)), 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Age Limit Rating 1.01 160.59 160.67 ``` ::: ::: ::: tip `Limit` and `Rating` are almost perfectly correlated: their coefficients become unstable. This motivates **ridge regression** (next lecture). ::: # Linear vs. KNN Regression ## KNN Regression - To predict at $x_0$, average the responses of the $K$ closest training points: $\hat f(x_0) = \dfrac1K\sum_{x_i\in\mathcal N_0} y_i$. - Small $K$: very flexible (low bias, high variance). Large $K$: smooth (high bias, low variance). ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} knn_reg <- function(xtrain, ytrain, xtest, k) { xtrain <- as.matrix(xtrain); xtest <- as.matrix(xtest) apply(xtest, 1, function(x0) { d <- sqrt(colSums((t(xtrain) - x0)^2)) mean(ytrain[order(d)[1:k]]) }) } ``` ::: ## KNN Fits for $K = 1$ and $K = 9$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750); n <- 100 xtr <- runif(n, 1, 6); ytr <- sin(xtr) + 0.2 * xtr + rnorm(n, sd = 0.4) grid <- seq(1, 6, length = 400) par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) for (k in c(1, 9)) { plot(xtr, ytr, pch = 1, col = "gray40", main = paste("K =", k), xlab = "x", ylab = "y") lines(grid, knn_reg(xtr, ytr, grid, k), col = "#003366", lwd = 3, type = "s") lines(grid, sin(grid) + 0.2 * grid, col = "red", lwd = 2, lty = 2) } ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/03-regression/unnamed-chunk-22-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ## Linear Regression vs. KNN as the Dimension Grows ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(4750) sim_mse <- function(p, k, n = 100, ntest = 500) { Xtr <- matrix(runif(n * p, -1, 1), n); Xte <- matrix(runif(ntest * p, -1, 1), ntest) ftrue <- function(X) 2 * X[, 1] + sin(3 * X[, 1]) # only X1 matters ytr <- ftrue(Xtr) + rnorm(n, sd = .5); yte <- ftrue(Xte) + rnorm(ntest, sd = .5) c(knn = mean((yte - knn_reg(Xtr, ytr, Xte, k))^2), lm = mean((yte - cbind(1, Xte) %*% coef(lm(ytr ~ Xtr)))^2)) } res <- sapply(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 10, 20), function(p) sim_mse(p, k = 9)) matplot(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 10, 20), t(res), type = "b", pch = 19, lwd = 3, col = c("#00A087", "black"), lty = 1, log = "x", xlab = "number of predictors p", ylab = "test MSE", main = "Curse of dimensionality") legend("topleft", c("KNN (K = 9)", "linear regression"), col = c("#00A087", "black"), lwd = 3, bty = "n") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](./images/03-regression/unnamed-chunk-23-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: alert KNN suffers from the **curse of dimensionality**: in high dimensions, the $K$ nearest neighbors are far away. ::: ## Summary ::: instructions - Least squares = projection: $\hat\bbeta = (\bX^\T\bX)^{-1}\bX^\T\by$ (computed via QR). - SEs, CIs, $t$ and $F$ tests describe *sampling variability*, which we can also see by simulation. - Dummy variables, interactions (hierarchy!), polynomial terms extend the linear model. - Diagnose: non-linearity, heteroscedasticity, outliers, leverage, collinearity (VIF). - Parametric (linear) vs. nonparametric (KNN): bias-variance and the curse of dimensionality. ::: [Interactive app: [Regression Shiny app](http://dna.mscsnet.mu.edu:3838/mlab/Regression/)]{.small}

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
